---
title: Formalization notes for Fermat's Last Theorem
description: Planning notes for the polynomial and regular-prime targets in index.qmd.
---

The [human chapter](index.qmd) describes polynomial proofs by descent, Mason–Stothers, and Riemann–Hurwitz, followed by Kummer's two cases for regular primes. The paired sidecar tracks the targets in that chapter.

The primitive solution predicate uses Bézout coprimality for each pair of coordinates. This expresses that the two coordinates generate the unit ideal. The predicate is defined for any natural exponent, and the subsequent theorems impose their own bounds.

The integer exponent-four result uses Mathlib's `not_fermat_42`. The polynomial proof via Mason–Stothers uses `Polynomial.abc`. The infinite descent proof uses the cyclotomic factorization and a minimal maximum coordinate degree. With $u_0^n = z - x$ and $u_1^n = z - \zeta x$, the difference $u_1^n - u_0^n$ equals $(1 - \zeta)x$.

For the cyclotomic coprimality statement, the allowed positive-characteristic case requires interpreting the coefficient ring generated by the root of unity as the image of the integer evaluation map. Keep the comparison with the characteristic-zero cyclotomic integers explicit when using it in Kummer's argument.

For the [prime-power congruence](index.qmd#lem-pth-power-congruence), first lift the residue of $\alpha$ to an integer $r$. Choose $a=r^p$ for the two congruences modulo $\lambda^p$. Fermat's little theorem gives $a\equiv r\pmod{\lambda}$, and raising to the $p$-th power lifts this last congruence to $\lambda^p$.

::: {#thm-dedekind-weil-divisor}
## Fractional ideals and Weil divisors

For the [Dedekind domain recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-dedekind), index Weil divisors by the nonzero prime ideals of a Dedekind domain $R$. The exponent of a prime in a nonzero fractional ideal gives an integer. These exponents have finite support, add under ideal multiplication, and recover the ideal by taking the product of prime powers. This defines the group isomorphism for Weil divisors. In the field case the index set is empty and the group is trivial.
:::

::: {#lem-dedekind-principal-order}
## Local orders of principal ideals

In the [Dedekind domain recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-dedekind), the order of a nonzero rational function at a nonzero prime equals the prime exponent of the principal fractional ideal it generates. Mathlib writes the valuation multiplicatively. The exponential of the negative ideal exponent gives that multiplicative valuation.
:::

::: {#prp-dedekind-spectrum-local-rings}
## Points and local rings of an affine Dedekind scheme

For the [Dedekind domain recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-dedekind), the generic point is the zero prime, and its residue field is canonically the fraction field. Every other point is closed and has a discrete valuation ring as its stalk. When the coordinate ring is a field, the generic point is also closed and its stalk is a field. At a nonzero prime the order on the stalk, expressed multiplicatively, is the inverse adic valuation on the fraction field. Taking its logarithm gives the usual additive order.
:::

For the [Picard group comparison](index.qmd#rem-scheme-dedekind), the height-one primes correspond to codimension-one points, with matching orders on rational functions. If $D_I$ records the prime exponents of a fractional ideal $I$, then the invertible sheaf $\mathcal O(-D_I)$ has $I$ as its global rational sections. Its class is the image of $[I]$ under the isomorphism $\operatorname{Cl}(R)\cong\operatorname{Pic}(\operatorname{Spec}R)$.

::: {#thm-fermat-function-field-genus}
## Genus of the Fermat function field

For the [Fermat genus calculation](index.qmd#prp-fermat-genus), let $F = k(x,y)$ with $x$ transcendental over a field $k$ of characteristic zero and $x^n + y^n = 1$ for $n > 0$. The homogeneous Fermat polynomial has no common nonzero zero of its partial derivatives over an algebraic closure. Tau Ceti's plane curve genus theorem gives $g(F) = (n-1)(n-2)/2$ and shows that $k$ is the exact constant field. For the [geometric Fermat theorem](index.qmd#thm-flt-geometric), the normalized coordinates would put this field inside $k(t)$, which has genus zero. Riemann–Hurwitz excludes that inclusion when $n \ge 3$.
:::

::: {#def-fermat-projective-scheme}
## The projective Fermat scheme

For the [projective Fermat curve](index.qmd#prp-fermat-genus), take the homogeneous quotient of $k[X,Y,Z]$ by $(X^n+Y^n-Z^n)$ and form its projective spectrum. This gives a closed subscheme of $\mathbb{P}^2_k$ and a proper morphism to $\operatorname{Spec}k$. Its three coordinate opens cover it. Over algebraically closed constants of characteristic zero and for $n>0$, dehomogenizing at $Z$ preserves degree and yields an irreducible equation, so the homogeneous coordinate ring is a domain and the projective scheme is integral.
:::

::: {#prp-fermat-projective-smooth}
## Smooth charts of the projective Fermat scheme

For the [projective Fermat curve](index.qmd#prp-fermat-genus), the degree-zero localization at each coordinate identifies with the quotient by the corresponding dehomogenized polynomial. A polynomial in two variables can be homogenized to prove surjectivity. For injectivity, homogenize the multiple of the dehomogenized equation and cancel powers of the inverted coordinate using primality of the homogeneous equation. The polynomial and its two partial derivatives generate the unit ideal in each chart, so the Jacobian criterion gives smoothness of relative dimension one on the projective scheme.
:::

::: {#lem-curve-extension-and-infinity-coordinates}
## Extension from a dense open and coordinates at infinity

For the [projective curve recall](index.qmd#rem-scheme-curves-recall), a morphism into a proper scheme extends uniquely from a dense open of an integral curve with discrete valuation rings at its codimension-one points. On the chart at infinity, if $M$ is the maximum coordinate degree, the reflected polynomials $s^M p_i(s^{-1})$ generate the unit ideal and satisfy the same homogeneous equations. A leading coefficient gives a nonzero coordinate at $s=0$.

For a nonconstant map to a plane curve of degree $n$, the coordinates give a pullback of $\mathcal O_C(1)$ of degree $M$. Since $\deg\mathcal O_C(1)=n$, the map degree satisfies $M=n\deg\pi$. For a direct map to $\mathbb P^1$ the corresponding line bundle has degree one.
:::

::: {#thm-tame-hurwitz-function-fields}
## Canonical divisors and tame Riemann–Hurwitz

For the [Riemann–Hurwitz recall](index.qmd#thm-riemann-hurwitz-recall), use divisors of Weil differentials over algebraically closed constants of characteristic zero. The canonical divisor has degree $2g-2$. Pulling it to the extension adds the tame different, whose coefficient at a place is $e_P-1$. Every place has degree one. For a genus-zero cover of degree $d$, the preimage of a set of $s$ places therefore has at least $sd-(2d-2)$ places.
:::

In the [Mason–Hurwitz argument](index.qmd#rem-mason-hurwitz-bridge), the point at infinity of the source contributes to the three fibres if its image is $0$, $1$, or $\infty$. This gives the stated upper bound of the radical degree plus one.

::: {#lem-kummer-local-congruence}
## Local congruences for Kummer’s unit lemma

For the [proof of Kummer’s unit lemma](index.qmd#rem-kummer-unit-proof), suppose $u$ is congruent to an integer modulo $p$. Fermat’s little theorem gives $u^{p-1}=1+pb$ with $b$ integral. Since $p$ is odd, the norm of $u^{p-1}$ is one. Expanding the norm modulo $p^2$ shows that $p$ divides the trace of $b$. Every conjugate of $b$ has the same residue modulo $\lambda$, so the trace reduces to $(p-1)b$. Thus $\lambda$ divides $b$ and $\lambda^p$ divides $u^{p-1}-1$.

Set $U=u^{p-1}$ and take $r^p=U$. Dividing $(\lambda X+1)^p-U$ coefficientwise by $\lambda^p$ gives a monic integral polynomial vanishing at $(r-1)/\lambda$.

For $p=3$, the congruence hypothesis implies $u=\pm1$ by Mathlib’s classification of cubic cyclotomic units congruent to integers modulo $\lambda^2$. Cubing the six units $\pm\zeta_3^j$ gives exactly the two values $\pm1$.
:::

::: {#lem-kummer-extension-unramified}
## Unramifiedness of the Kummer extension

For the [proof of Kummer’s unit lemma](index.qmd#rem-kummer-unit-proof), a nontrivial automorphism of $K(r)/K$ sends $r$ to $\zeta_p^j r$ with $1\le j<p$. Its difference on the integral element $(r-1)/\lambda$ is $((\zeta_p^j-1)/\lambda)r$. The first factor is a cyclotomic unit, and $r$ is an integral unit because $r^p=U$. The difference is a unit, so it cannot vanish modulo any proper prime ideal. This makes the inertia group trivial at every finite prime.
:::

For the class-number step of the [unit lemma](index.qmd#lem-kummer-unit), a cyclic extension of degree $d$ supplies all $d$th powers as idèle-class norms. If $d$ is coprime to the class number, each idèle class is a product of such a power and a class represented by local units at every finite place. Unramifiedness makes these local units norms, and all infinite places of the base are complex. The first fundamental inequality then forces $d=1$. Thus $U=u^{p-1}$ has a $p$th root $r$ in $K$, and $u/r$ and its inverse are integral because their $p$th powers are integral units.

::: {#prp-bernoulli-numerator-test-below-100}
## Bernoulli numerator tests below 100

For the [Bernoulli criterion](index.qmd#rem-bernoulli-regular), among odd primes below 100, some numerator in $B_2,B_4,\ldots,B_{p-3}$ is divisible by $p$ exactly for $37$, $59$, and $67$. The witnesses are $B_{32}$, $B_{44}$, and $B_{58}$, respectively. Lean checks the finite table using Mathlib’s rational Bernoulli recurrence.
:::

::: {#prp-cyclotomic-differentials}
## Differentials of the prime cyclotomic integers

For the [arithmetic surface recall](index.qmd#rem-arithmetic-surface), write $B=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$ and $\lambda=1-\zeta_p$. In the monogenic presentation of $B$, $d\zeta_p$ generates the module of relative differentials with relation $\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)d\zeta_p=0$. Differentiating $(X-1)\Phi_p(X)=X^p-1$ shows that $(\zeta_p-1)\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)=p\zeta_p^{p-1}$. The derivative therefore generates $(\lambda^{p-2})$, which is also the different ideal. For odd $p$, the cover is étale precisely at primes of $B$ away from $p$.
:::

::: {#prp-cyclotomic-cover-scheme}
## The cyclotomic cover over the integer spectrum

For the [arithmetic surface recall](index.qmd#rem-arithmetic-surface), the structural morphism from the spectrum of a number ring to $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb{Z}$ is finite and flat. Over the basic open $D(p)$, the prime cyclotomic morphism is the spectrum map of $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]\to B[1/p]$. For odd $p$, this map is étale by the differential computation.
:::
